records.name_note: NC State's dedicated page for this exact name lists previous names Epiphyllopsis gaertneri, Hatiora gaertneri, Rhipsalis gaertneri and Schlumbergera gaertneri, so this taxon has been filed under Hatiora, Schlumbergera and Rhipsalis; no care text is imported from any Schlumbergera page. The page's "is often confused with:" module names Schlumbergera russelliana, Schlumbergera truncata and Schlumbergera x buckleyi, and its description says the Easter cactus is often confused with Thanksgiving cactus and Christmas cactus. Only one admissible source was read, so there is no split between sources on the common name: the page's Common Name(s) list (Easter Cactus, Holiday Cactus, Whitesun) is alphabetized and its order matches the page-title parenthetical, and the description opens with "Easter cactus".
records.toxicity_detail: Scoped to cats and dogs by NC State's Tags list, which includes both "non-toxic for cats" and "non-toxic for dogs" (and "pet friendly"). The same Tags block also carries: houseplant, showy flowers, low maintenance, interiorscape, cactus, fantz, epiphytic, container plant, succulent, herbaceous perennial, perennial, long lived, ornamentals, humidity tolerant, dry soils tolerant, spring flowers, red fruits, florist plant. The Plant Type field lists four values: Epiphyte, Herbaceous Perennial, Houseplant, Succulent. The page carries no Poison block, no poisonous-parts list, no symptom list, no severity rating and no handling warning, so nothing is stated about human toxicity or edibility, and the non-toxic tags are tags, not a dose or symptom statement. Only one admissible source was read, so no disagreement on scope could be checked. Nothing here is drawn from Easter Lily (Lilium longiflorum) or the Echinopsis 'Easter lily cactus'.
records.cool_rest_note: Cultivation condition, not a watering rule: NC State says temperatures should range from 60 to 75 degrees Fahrenheit, but cooler temperatures of 50 degrees Fahrenheit in late winter will promote blooming. The same page adds that the plants are sensitive to day length and need long uninterrupted nights to set flower buds.
unknowns: Only NC State (plants.ces.ncsu.edu) was successfully read. The RHS URL guessed for this species returned 404, Clemson HGIC returned a 403 bot block, and MoBot's PlantFinder host was not reachable from the sandbox, so no second admissible source could confirm or contradict any field. Nothing was borrowed from a parent, genus or sibling page.
chill_damage_f left null: NC State gives a recommended range (60 to 75 F) and a USDA zone list, neither of which is a damage-onset temperature.
day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max left null: NC State gives one undifferentiated 60 to 75 F range and does not split it into day and night.
humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max left null: the page says it prefers high humidity but gives no percentage.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good left null: the page says bright, indirect light and gives no foot-candle figure. direct_sun_hours_max left null: the only hour figure (2-6 hours) is inside NC State's structured Light category value and no species-specific prose states a direct-sun hour limit. The prose also warns that scorched leaves can result from direct sunlight, especially during the hottest parts of the day.

outdoor_sun_exposure is part_shade only, from NC State's structured Light field 'Partial Shade'; the prose also says the plant can be placed outdoors in a shady location for the warm summer months. No source read supports full_sun, part_sun or full_shade.

soil_drainage is moderate because the prose asks for a moist, well-drained cactus mix and the structured field is Good Drainage plus Occasionally Dry; the 'cactus' label is not treated as evidence of fast drainage. soil_base cactus_succulent comes from the page's 'cactus potting mix' wording.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0); the acid band is open-ended so gives no floor, and the neutral band's closed top of 8.0 could not be checked against RHS for alkaline tolerance.

water_regime keep_moist rests on the prose 'keep the soil moist but avoid overwatering'. Counterpoints on the same page: winter watering is reduced during dormancy, the page warns that overwatering or underwatering makes stems drop segments, and root rot is listed as a problem; the structured Soil Drainage includes Occasionally Dry and the tags include dry soils tolerant (a tolerance trait, not used for water_regime). The page gives no day interval or dry-down depth, so water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est and water_estimate_basis are null.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months and fertilize_strength left null: the page says only to fertilize once a month when actively growing; that is a word cadence with no stated number of days, no named months and no dilution strength.

is_edible left null: the page does not address eating the plant or its fruit (it only describes the fruit as dull red, oblong and 15 mm long). attracts_pollinators left null: no Attracts field or pollinator statement on the page.
toxic_to_pets=false rests on NC State's 'non-toxic for cats' and 'non-toxic for dogs' tags; the page has no Poison block, symptom list or severity rating, and only one admissible source was read.
mature size comes from NC State's prose and Dimensions block (Height 0 ft. 6 in. - 1 ft. 0 in.; Width 1 ft. 6 in. - 2 ft. 0 in.), converted to inches (6-12 tall, 18-24 wide).

Symptoms include mouth and throat irritation, drooling, vomiting, difficulty breathing, and swallowing."; Poison Toxic Principle: Calcium oxalate crystals; Causes Contact Dermatitis: No; Poison Part: Leaves, Stems. The page header line says "This plant has medium severity poison characteristics." Separate Problems field values on the same page: Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs. Plant Type values: Epiphyte, Houseplant, Perennial, Vine. The hashtag Tags line carries #problem for dogs, #problem for cats, #problem for children and #poisonous if ingested. Handling and description prose: "This plant is toxic if ingested. Exercise caution in the presence of children and pets." The page makes no sap or skin-contact claim beyond Contact Dermatitis: No. Only NC State was available, so no cross-source disagreement on scope could be checked.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on the primary common name. NC State's dedicated page for Phlebodium aureum leads its page-title parenthetical with Blue Star Fern, while RHS's dedicated page titles the species "golden polypody" and lists hare's foot fern and rabbit's foot fern as other common names; Blue Star Fern was chosen because it leads the NC State page. Older sources file the species as Polypodium aureum (NC State "Previously known as", RHS synonym). 'Davana' is a cultivar name (NC State) and 'Blue Star' is a cultivar name (RHS has a separate 'Blue Star' cultivar page), so neither is a species name. NC State's name list also includes Rabbits Foot Fern, but Clemson applies rabbit's foot fern to Davallia solida var. fejeensis, a different record in this catalog; no Davallia care is used here.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail left null: NC State's page has no Poison section or cat/dog tags, and no admissible source found that names Phlebodium aureum (or Polypodium aureum) with cats or dogs. Clemson's pet-safe houseplant page and the UF/IFAS, UGA and UMD pet-plant pages checked do not name this species. Missouri Botanical Garden (plantfinder.mobot.org) could not be loaded from this environment (connection and certificate failures), so no MoBot page was read; no UF/IFAS or Clemson dedicated page for this species was found.

chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note and all day/night temperature fields null: neither NC State nor RHS gives a damage-onset or houseplant temperature range for this species. NC State's USDA zones 8b-13b are a hardiness rating, not a damage onset. RHS's H1B rating is UK-calibrated and its Cultivation text does not give a temperature.
humidity_need left null: NC State says ideal conditions include medium to high humidity, which straddles average and high, and gives no percentages.

light_fc_min, light_fc_good, direct_sun_hours_max null: NC State's Light tags carry a generic hours legend (not species prose) and no foot-candle figure; RHS says best grown out of direct sunlight but gives no hours. NC State's prose also says partial sun is ideal, but its structured Light tags are Dappled Sunlight, Deep shade and Partial Shade, so part_sun is not added. Dappled Sunlight and Partial Shade map to part_shade. These outdoor values are for landscape use (native to FL, GA and AL, hardy to zone 8b), separate from houseplant care.

soil_base left null: NC State says a loose, organic substrate with an acid pH, and RHS lists Loam; neither names a potting-mix type that maps cleanly to an enum without inference. NC State soil textures Sand and Shallow Rocky do not make drainage fast.
soil_drainage moderate rests on NC State's Good Drainage plus Moist pair, 'moist but not soggy', and RHS 'Moist but well-drained'.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max null: NC State's Acid (<6.0) band is open-ended and gives no usable floor or ceiling, while RHS lists pH Neutral, so the sources are not consistent.

water_regime dry_surface_between comes from RHS's watering instruction (water generously once the pot is drying out) plus NC State's 'tolerates drying out between waterings'. NC State's 'moist but not soggy substrate' is a counterpoint that could read as keep_moist; no numeric dry-down depth or interval is stated, so water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm and both day estimates are null.

fertilizer fields null: no admissible source read states a fertilizing schedule or dilution for this species. RHS's Cultivation text points to a shared Epiphytic Ferns advice page, which is not species evidence.
is_edible null: no source read addresses eating. attracts_pollinators null: NC State's Attracts field lists Songbirds only, which is not pollination.

Mature size uses NC State's own Dimensions block (height 2-4 ft, width 3-6 ft). RHS disagrees: Max Height 0.5-1 metres (19.7-39.4 in) and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in), with time to maturity 2-5 years. NC State's width is far larger than RHS's spread, so spread is uncertain.
The Clemson Indoor Ferns page and other multi-species pages were not used for taxon-specific content.

outdoor_sun_exposure is part_shade only. NC State's Light field also carries 'Deep shade (Less than 2 hours to no direct sunlight)', which would map to full_shade, but RHS's structured Position field lists Partial shade only, and NC State itself files Heavy Shade under Resistance To Challenges (a tolerance, not the preferred exposure), so full_shade is not used.

records.name_note: Sources lead differently. NC State's dedicated page is headed with the binomial; its rendered Common Name(s) list is alphabetized and begins Argentinian Vervain, and its page-title parenthetical gives the same eight names in the same order, but its Description opens with Tall verbena. RHS's dedicated page gives purple top as its common name (the page title reads Verbena bonariensis | purple top), and its Other common names list includes tall verbena. Tall Verbena is used as NC State's Description opener; both sources also carry Purple Top and Argentinian Vervain. NC State's common-name list also carries Brazilian Vervain, its is-often-confused-with module lists Verbena brasiliensis, and RHS lists Verbena brasiliensis as a misapplied synonym; nothing was taken from brasiliensis, aristigera or cultivar pages.
unknowns: No toxicity or edibility statement found on the NC State or RHS pages for this taxon, so toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail and is_edible are null.

Weed status as worded: NC State lists Plant Type Annual, Perennial, Weed; says it has naturalized in the United States from North Carolina to Florida and west to Texas, that it is a weed that spreads by volunteer seedlings, and that some sources have labeled it "invasive." RHS warns it may have the potential to become a nuisance due to prolific self-seeding if not well managed.
Range: NC State says it is a tender perennial hardy from zones 7 to 11 and grown as an annual in cooler climates (its USDA zone field is 7a-11b). RHS gives bare rating H4 (UK).
NC State advises leaving dead stems standing (cut back to 12 to 24 inches) because native bees nest in the dead, hollow stems.
soil_drainage is moderate from NC State's Good Drainage + Moist + Occasionally Dry tags (Clay is in its texture list) and RHS 'moist but well-drained or well-drained'.

soil_ph_min/max null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0); the Acid and Alkaline bands are open-ended, so no floor or ceiling can be read off them, and RHS lists Acid or Alkaline or Neutral.

water_regime null: NC State only says it tolerates average to dry conditions (a tolerance, not a watering instruction); RHS's moisture field describes soil. No watering statement found. Water/fertilizer interval fields null for an in-ground perennial.

direct_sun_hours_max null: the only hour figures are NC State's generic light-category labels. NC State's structured Light field also lists Partial Shade, but RHS's Position lists Full sun only and NC State's prose names only full sun, so part_shade is not used.
Size differs by source: NC State 2-5 ft tall, 2-3 ft wide (used); RHS Max Height 1.5-2.5 metres and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres.

Temperature, humidity, light fc and chill damage: no admissible-source statement found. is_houseplant is false: no source frames it as a houseplant; NC State files it as an outdoor annual/perennial for zones 7a-11b.
Fertilizer: none stated on the sources read.
Pages used: NC State and RHS only; other admissible domains (MoBot, Clemson, UF/IFAS etc.) were not consulted.

soil_drainage fast rests on NC State's statement that good drainage is essential and that crown rot occurs in wet, poorly drained soils, plus Sand and Shallow Rocky textures and the Occasionally Dry tag; it is not based on the bare Good Drainage tag. RHS gives Moisture: Well-drained only.

Life cycle: NC State's Life Cycle field lists Annual, Biennial and Perennial, its Plant Type lists Annual and Herbaceous Perennial, and its tags include #biennial and #short lived. RHS calls it an evergreen perennial. Expect it to need replacing; NC State recommends division every 2-3 years.

Sun: NC State lists only full sun and RHS says Position Full sun; no part_sun or part_shade is recorded. direct_sun_hours_max is null because NC State's 6-or-more-hours text is its generic light-category legend, not species prose.
Pollinators: NC State's Attracts field lists Butterflies and its Wildlife Value says Attracts bees, butterflies; its Play Value also lists Attracts Pollinators.

Temperature, humidity, light_fc, fertilizer and chill_damage_f are null because no admissible source for this exact species gives them; RHS's H6 hardiness rating is not a damage-onset temperature. is_houseplant is false: no source frames it as a houseplant, and NC State files it as an outdoor groundcover for zones 3a-8b.

records.name_note: Sources split on which common name leads. RHS's dedicated Helleborus niger page carries Christmas rose as its title and subtitle. NC State's Common Name(s) list and its Description both lead with Black Hellebore ("Black hellebore is a winter-blooming evergreen perennial in the Ranunculaceae family."), and its prose adds that the plants are often called Christmas roses. NC State says the name lenten rose is historically associated with H. orientalis. Christmas Rose was chosen as the common name, following RHS.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension Plant Toolbox (Helleborus niger page). Its top-of-page line, 'This plant has medium severity poison characteristics.', points ('See below') to the 'Poisonous to Humans' block, where the severity rating sits: Poison Severity: Medium. Poison Symptoms: TOXIC ONLY IF LARGE QUANTITIES EATEN. SKIN IRRITATION MINOR, OR LASTING ONLY FOR A FEW MINUTES. Burning of mouth and throat, salivation, vomiting, abdominal cramping, diarrhea, nervous symptoms, depression. Skin irritation after contact with cell sap. Poison Toxic Principle: Cardiac glycosides, saponins, Protoanemonin. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part: Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems (NC State lists Bark although its Plant Type is Herbaceous Perennial). The page's Problems field lists Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs and Problem for Horses, and its Tags carry #problem for cats, #problem for dogs and #problem for horses. Those cat and dog tags are separate from the human-scoped Poison block, and they are the only basis here for the pet scope. NC State's Plant Type field lists Ground Cover, Herbaceous Perennial, Poisonous. Its Insects, Diseases, Other Plant Problems prose says separately: 'The leaves and roots are poisonous.' Its Description adds that the scientific name comes from the Greek words 'helein', meaning injures, and 'bora', meaning food, referring to the toxic properties when the plant is eaten. RHS's Potentially harmful field reads 'Harmful if eaten; skin irritant. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling.' Its Pets line says 'Harmful if eaten; skin irritant.' and names no particular animal, and the field refers readers to the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information regarding pets. NC State's 'TOXIC ONLY IF LARGE QUANTITIES EATEN' qualifier (human block) and RHS's unqualified 'Harmful if eaten' both appear on the sources. They differ in emphasis, and neither restricts the hazard to one plant part in the way a fruit-only rating would.
unknowns: is_houseplant is false: no admissible source frames this species as a houseplant. NC State's Container Landscape Location and the 'container plant' tag are outdoor-use tags, not an indoor-culture statement.

water_regime left null: RHS gives a structured Moisture field of 'Moist but well-drained', while NC State's Soil Drainage tags are Good Drainage and Occasionally Dry, and its Resistance To Challenges field lists Drought and Dry Soil. Neither source gives a watering statement, so no regime token is supported. The water_* day and dry-down fields are also null because this is an in-ground perennial and no source frames watering that way.

soil_drainage is moderate: NC State's Good Drainage with Occasionally Dry tags and RHS's 'Moist but well-drained' are consistent with the middle of the scale. Neither source asks for consistently wet soil or sharp, sandy drainage.

soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists the open-ended Alkaline (>8.0) band plus Neutral (6.0-8.0), and RHS lists 'Alkaline or Neutral', so alkaline soils are acceptable and no ceiling can be set. soil_ph_min 6.0 is the closed floor of NC State's Neutral band. NC State lists no Acid band, and RHS gives only 'Alkaline or Neutral'.

outdoor_sun_exposure covers part_shade and full_shade only. NC State's Dappled Sunlight and Partial Shade tags map to part_shade and its Deep shade tag to full_shade; its prose says 'partial to full shade'. RHS's Position is 'Partial shade', which also fits part_shade. No source states full_sun or part_sun. direct_sun_hours_max is null because the 2-6 hour figure inside NC State's Light tag is a site-wide legend, not species prose.

Size conflict: NC State's Dimensions block (Height 9-12 in, Width 12-18 in) is used as the anchor. RHS lists Max Height 0.1-0.5 metres and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in), a wider range that is not used.
Foliage conflict: NC State tags the plant Broadleaf Evergreen and Evergreen, while RHS lists Foliage 'Semi evergreen'. This does not change any field.

toxic_to_pets is true on the strength of NC State's Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags only. RHS's Pets line names no animal and is not used as support. NC State's Poison block is human-scoped, and its full Poison Part list (Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems) is reproduced in toxicity_detail.

is_edible is false on the strength of RHS's 'Harmful if eaten' and NC State's poison block (with its 'TOXIC ONLY IF LARGE QUANTITIES EATEN' qualifier). No source describes the plant as food. NC State also notes the generic name's Greek roots refer to toxic properties when the plant is eaten.

Invasiveness note, recorded only as stated: NC State says the NC Invasive Plant Council regards all hellebores as potentially invasive, although the threat is low. NC State also says the plant spreads through self-seeding and self-seeds easily.

Taxon scope: nothing was taken from the H. orientalis, H. foetidus or H. x hybridus pages. NC State names Lenten Rose in its list but ties the name historically to H. orientalis, and RHS's bear's foot alias is also shared with H. foetidus. Neither contrast was cited from the other species' pages.

Not found in the admissible sources, so left null: chill damage, day and night temperature ranges, humidity, footcandle light levels, fertilizing. Hardiness zones (NC State 3a-8b, RHS H7) are survival ratings, not damage-onset temperatures. MoBot, Clemson, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD and UGA were not consulted for a dedicated page for this species.

toxic_to_pets is null: NC State prints no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags for this species. Pet toxicity on the landed A. millefolium Yarrow record is not imported.

is_edible is true: NC State's Edibility line says 'The leaves can be eaten raw or cooked.' (leaves are the only part named), and its Plant Type list carries the Edible tag. No other part is addressed and no preparation times are given. The page prints no toxicity statement either way.

soil_drainage is moderate: average well-drained soil, Clay in the texture list, Good Drainage plus Occasionally Dry tags, and a root-rot-from-overwatering warning. The page gives no wet-tolerance and also lists dry soil and drought tolerance, so the landed Yarrow record's fast is not copied. A bare 'well-drained' reading would be ambiguous.

soil_ph_max is null: NC State's Neutral (6.0-8.0) band is the only pH field. A ceiling cannot be checked against RHS's pH field, so none is set. soil_ph_min 6.0 is the floor of the Neutral band only; NC State lists no Acid band for this plant.

water_regime is null: the page says 'Do not over-fertilize or water' and 'Overwatering can lead to root rot', plus heat, humidity and drought tolerance. These are cautions, not a dry-down or moisture-level instruction that maps to one enum token.
No fertilizer interval, strength or months are stated; 'Do not over-fertilize' is the only fertilizing text.
direct_sun_hours_max is null: the only hours figure is the Light field's 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)', which is open-ended and is the generic category wording.
NC State's Flower Bloom Time lists Fall, Spring and Summer; its Description says flowers appear most of the summer if deadheaded. Not a schema field.

Cultivar content on the page ('Altgold', 'Cloth of Gold', 'Coronation Gold', 'Gold Plate', the phytophthora-resistance sentence about 'some cultivars', and the cultivar heights 'Altgold' Shorter cultivar, 2' and 'Cloth of Gold' Taller cultivar - 5') is not species evidence and is not used. NC State gives no temperature ranges or damage onset (only USDA zones 3a-9b and a heat-tolerance statement), no humidity level (only "It is heat, humidity and drought tolerant."), no light in foot-candles, and does not address houseplant status.

is_houseplant is false: NC State does not address houseplant status; it files the species as an outdoor herbaceous perennial for USDA zones 3a-9b, for the border, mass planting, containers and rock gardens.
